checks.claim: Key: a newborn grips a finger placed in her palm on the day she is born (palmar grasp reflex, present at birth)
checks.note: Grokipedia: elicited by stroking or placing an object in the palm; 'fully present at birth in healthy term infants'. AAP (healthychildren.org) chart agrees.

checks.claim: Context: the grasp reflex fades by about six months
checks.note: Grokipedia: disappears between 4 and 6 months, 'usually absent by 5 to 6 months'; AAP chart: 5-6 months. 'By about six months' is fair.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: reach out to grab a toy (not a day-one behaviour)
checks.note: CDC 6-month milestone: 'Reaches to grab a toy she wants'. Newborns make jerky 'pre-reaching' arm movements (von Hofsten) but do not reach and grab a toy; first successful grasps come about 4 months (PMC reviews). Not defensible as a newborn ability.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: lift her arms to be picked up (not a day-one behaviour)
checks.note: CDC 9-month milestone: 'Lifts arms up to be picked up'.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: wave bye-bye (not a day-one behaviour; taught)
checks.note: CDC 1-year milestone: 'Waves bye-bye'; the 9-month page tells parents to teach the baby to wave bye-bye.

checks.claim: Context: these come 'many months later' as she grows and learns from people around her
checks.note: 6, 9 and 12 months respectively; 'many months later' is fair even for reaching (first grasps about 4 months, CDC milestone 6 months).

checks.claim: Framing: a newborn reflex counted as an instinct
checks.note: Wikipedia: instinctive behaviours in humans include many of the primitive reflexes. Fine at 5th-grade level.

checks.claim: Key: web spinning is inborn (instinct)
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'Newly emerged spiders construct functional webs without observation or practice'. Isolation-rearing studies of Araneus diadematus: spiderlings reared alone still built functional orb webs (search of archive.org biostor 215130; Witt et al. 1972 via Reed College page).

checks.claim: Wrong choice: its mother taught it
checks.note: The female 'dies shortly after oviposition, often by early winter'; the young hatch in spring, so no teaching is possible. Buglife's garden cross spider page (seen in search; direct fetch 404) says the same: she dies in late autumn before the spiderlings hatch the following May.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: it watched older spiders at work
checks.note: Functional webs are built without observation; isolation-reared spiders build them.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: it learned from its brothers and sisters
checks.note: Garden spiderlings do cluster together for about a week after hatching, and one study found isolated spiders' webs differed measurably from communally reared ones, but isolated spiders still built working orb webs, so the skill is not learned from siblings. Not defensible at this level.

checks.claim: Stem: a garden spider's web is a wheel of silk threads for catching flies
checks.note: 'classic orb webs that are wheel-shaped'; catches 'flying insects such as flies, wasps, moths, and beetles'.

checks.claim: Context: the mother dies in late autumn, soon after laying her eggs
checks.note: Eggs laid September to November; female 'dies shortly after oviposition, often by early winter'; Buglife: she dies in late autumn before the spiderlings hatch.

checks.claim: Context: the young hatch the next spring and scatter to build webs of their own
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'Hatching occurs in spring, typically April to May'; spiderlings disperse by ballooning and build small early webs. Buglife and British Spiders (seen in search): spiderlings emerge from the egg sac in spring (May in the UK), cluster as a golden ball, then after about a week spread out and build their own small webs. (Some sources say the eggs hatch in autumn and the spiderlings overwinter inside the sac, emerging in spring; 'hatch the next spring' is the standard simplification and fair.)

checks.claim: Stem: hatchlings dig out of the nest, usually at night, and crawl to the sea; heading for the sea is an instinct
checks.note: FWC: hatchlings 'emerge primarily at night' and have 'an inborn tendency to move in the brightest direction'; Grokipedia Sea turtle: emerge 'often at night, by collectively excavating upward through the sand'.

checks.claim: Key: it knows the way with no one to teach it
checks.note: NPS: the female 'returns to the sea, leaving the nest untended'; hatchlings guided by instinct.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: it can follow its mother to the water
checks.note: The mother leaves weeks before hatching; nest untended.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: it can practise the crawl until it is fast
checks.note: Hatchlings head straight for the sea on emergence using inborn visual cues; no practice is involved and none would help them survive the dash.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: it can learn the way by trial and error
checks.note: Orientation is an inborn response to the brightest direction (and away from dark silhouettes), not trial-and-error learning. (Hatchlings may imprint on the natal beach's magnetic field for later return, but that is not how they find the sea.)

checks.claim: Context: the mother laid her eggs, covered them with sand and went back to the sea, leaving the nest untended
checks.note: NPS: 'The female comes ashore at night, digs a nest, lays her eggs, covers her eggs with sand, and returns to the sea, leaving the nest untended.'

checks.claim: Context: hatchlings crawl toward the brightest part of the sky, which on a dark beach lies over the sea
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'toward the brightest horizon reflecting moonlight or starlight over the ocean and away from dark silhouettes of dunes and vegetation, aided by beach slope'. NPS: 'the brightest horizon, which was the light from the sky reflecting off the ocean'. A fair simplification (it leaves out the silhouettes and slope cues but says nothing false).

checks.claim: Context: bright lights near a beach can fool them into crawling the wrong way
checks.note: FWC: artificial lighting 'is what often leads hatchlings astray'; NPS: lights 'disorient hatchling sea turtles, leading them astray', may draw them inland.

checks.claim: Key: looking both ways before crossing a road is learned (taught)
checks.note: CHOP: 'Teach children to look LEFT, RIGHT and then LEFT again before crossing a street'; children under 10 should not cross alone.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: sneezing when dust tickles the nose (an inborn reflex, not learned)
checks.note: Grokipedia: a protective reflex that clears irritants; triggers include dust. Seattle Children's lists sneezing among a newborn's normal protective reflexes (https://www.seattlechildrens.org/conditions/a-z/newborn-reflexes-and-behavior/).

checks.claim: Wrong choice: coughing when a crumb sticks in the throat (an inborn reflex)
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'a protective reflex mechanism to clear the airways of irritants ... and foreign particles', including food in choking. Seattle Children's lists coughing as a newborn's protective reflex.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: jerking a hand back from a hot pan (an inborn reflex)
checks.note: Grokipedia: touching a hot stove prompts 'an immediate retraction of the arm', 'an automatic protective mechanism' 'mediated entirely at the spinal cord level'. Grokipedia Instinct and Reflex count it as innate.

checks.claim: Context: children are taught to look left, right and left again before they cross a street
checks.note: True only where traffic drives on the right (the US drill, CHOP). In left-hand-traffic countries the drill is the reverse: the UK Green Cross Code teaches 'look right, look left, look right again' (Lancashire and Milton Keynes council road-safety sheets). The bank is written in British English and the next question is set on British doorsteps, so a British, Irish, Australian or Indian player would read this as wrong. Fix: 'Children are taught to look both ways, and then again, before they cross a street.'

checks.claim: Context: sneezing, coughing and snatching a hand back from heat are reflexes the body does by itself, with no lessons, to protect itself
checks.note: Reflexes are involuntary, innate and often protective (Grokipedia Reflex, Sneeze, Cough, Withdrawal reflex).

checks.claim: Key: a dog learns a trick by being rewarded each time it does it
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'Positive reinforcement dominates modern dog training'; treats lure and reward; 'give paw' ('shake') can be taught from 8-12 weeks. Trainers reward every time while teaching and thin the rewards later; 'each time' is fair for how the trick is learned.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: it is born with an instinct for it
checks.note: Sitting and pawing are natural movements, but doing them on a spoken command is trained. Not defensible as the answer to 'how does a dog come to do a trick like this'.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: it inherits the trick from its parents
checks.note: Learned skills are acquired characteristics, 'not passed on to offspring through reproduction'.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: it simply grows into it with age
checks.note: Tricks need training at any age; they do not appear by growing up.

checks.claim: Context: the owner gives a treat or praise each time it does the trick, and soon it does it on command
checks.note: Treats and praise are the standard rewards ('Verbal praise and petting act as low-intensity rewards').

checks.claim: Context: 'A trained dog's puppies are not born knowing its tricks, because a learned behaviour is not passed on to the young.'
checks.note: The first half is true, but the reason as worded is false: learned behaviour often IS passed on to the young, by teaching and copying. Pups that watched their trained mother search for narcotics learned the task faster (Slabbert and Rasa 1997, Applied Animal Behaviour Science 53: 309-316, cited in Fugazza et al. 2018, 'Social learning from conspecifics and humans in dog puppies', Scientific Reports, which also found 8-week-old puppies learn by watching); Grokipedia Dog training: 'Dogs acquire new behaviors through social learning by observing conspecifics or humans'. The same unit's blue-tit question teaches a learned habit spreading from bird to bird, and TEKS 5.13B's own learned example (orcas hunting in packs) is passed from mother to calf. What is not passed on is the trick at birth, through the genes. Fix: '...are not born knowing its tricks, because a learned behaviour is not inherited: each puppy has to learn the trick for itself.'

checks.claim: Stem: milk was once left on British doorsteps in glass bottles with thin foil caps; blue tits pecked through the caps to drink the cream
checks.note: Wikipedia: blue tits learned 'to open traditional British milk bottles with foil tops to access the cream underneath'. (Detail, not an error since the stem gives no date: the first record, Swaythling near Southampton in 1921, was of tits prising open WAXBOARD tops; the BTO's survey summary says so, and Grokipedia wrongly says foil for 1921. Foil caps came later and the habit is best known with them.)

checks.claim: Stem: the habit spread from town to town
checks.note: BTO summary of Fisher and Hinde's 1939-46 enquiry (British Birds 42: 347-357, 1949): the habit became widespread across England and parts of Wales, Scotland and Ireland; 'begun by comparatively few individual birds, and ... the vast majority then learned it in some way from others'. Nuance: by 1947 there were 89 records more than 25 km from any earlier one, so it was also re-invented independently in many places, and later work (Sherry and Galef 1984, 1990) argued birds may learn it from finding opened bottles rather than by imitation. 'Spread from town to town' describes the spread and claims no mechanism, so it stands.

checks.claim: Key: learning lets animals change their ways as things change
checks.note: Grokipedia Learning: learned behaviours 'offer flexibility for coping with variable or novel conditions', innate actions are 'rigid'.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: they can act right the very first time they try
checks.note: That is the mark of an instinct (performed without prior learning or experience), not of learning.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: they can pass new skills on through their eggs
checks.note: Acquired characteristics are not passed on through reproduction.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: they can get by without any instincts
checks.note: Birds still rely on many instincts; learning adds to them. Not defensible.

checks.claim: Context: instincts stay the same while learned behaviours can change to fit a changing world; a new skill is not passed on in an egg, each young bird must learn it
checks.note: Matches Grokipedia Learning (flexible vs rigid) and the acquired-characteristic rule. 'No instinct could have prepared a bird for a milk bottle' is rhetoric but fair: the pecking and tearing come from the tit's ordinary foraging, the target was new.

checks.claim: Key: her brown eyes came from her birth parents (eye colour is inherited)
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'a polygenic trait influenced by multiple genes', chiefly OCA2 and HERC2. Twin studies put its heritability at about 0.98 (Louisville Twin Study, Bito et al. 1997, cited in Twin Research). Many genes do not make it less inherited, so 'set by genes passed down from parents' is fair at this level. (A baby's eyes can darken in the first year as melanin builds, but the final colour is still genetic.)

checks.claim: Wrong choice: the language she speaks
checks.note: Internationally adopted children 'lose their birth language rapidly and become fluent speakers of their new language'; Ana, adopted as a newborn, learned her family's language.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: her skill at swimming
checks.note: 'The ability to do something well is an acquired characteristic'.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: the scar on her knee
checks.note: Scars are listed as acquired characteristics, not passed on.

checks.claim: Context: the language, the swimming and the scar came from her own life (the family that raised her, practice, an old fall)
checks.note: All three are acquired, not inherited.

checks.claim: Key: no, muscle built by work is not inherited
checks.note: 'The muscles acquired by a bodybuilder through physical training and diet' are acquired characteristics, 'not passed on to offspring through reproduction'. Grokipedia Lamarckism: modern genetics found no mechanism; epigenetic effects are limited and do not pass on built muscle.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: yes, children inherit what parents build
checks.note: This is the rejected Lamarckian idea.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: yes, if the work came before the boy's birth
checks.note: Timing makes no difference; Weismann's tail-cut mice never bore short-tailed young.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: no, a son inherits only from his mother
checks.note: Wrong reason: a child gets one allele of each gene from each parent; 'the zygote's genome ... comprises 50% maternal and 50% paternal DNA'.

checks.claim: Context: people once believed a blacksmith's strong arms could be handed down to his sons, but that idea proved wrong
checks.note: Grokipedia: Lamarck illustrated use and disuse with 'the robust forearms of blacksmiths', and 'robust musculature in blacksmith lineages' was taken as support for inheritance; the blacksmith-and-his-sons version is the stock textbook illustration of Lamarckism. Darwin too accepted inheritance of acquired traits (pangenesis). Rejected after Weismann and Mendelian genetics.

checks.claim: Context: a child inherits genes from both the mother and the father
checks.note: 'inherit two alleles per gene, one from each parent'.

unit_notes: 8 questions: 6 ok, 1 error, 1 uncertain. Error (4d7ce512e6): the dog context says flatly that 'a learned behaviour is not passed on to the young', which is false (learned behaviour is passed on by teaching and copying, as the blue-tit question in this very unit teaches) and clashes with TEKS 5.13B's orca example; say 'not inherited' instead. Uncertain (5707d900a7): 'look left, right and left again' is the right-hand-traffic drill; the UK Green Cross Code reverses it; say 'look both ways, and then again'. Checked and fine: the grasp reflex (present at birth, gone by 5-6 months; CDC ages for reaching 6 mo, arms up 9 mo, bye-bye 12 mo); garden spiderlings raised alone still build working orb webs (early silk can be shapeless, and the stem avoids 'first try'); hatchlings head for the brightest seaward horizon (they also turn away from dark dune silhouettes and use slope, which the context leaves out but does not contradict); no wrong choice in the turtle question is partly true. The milk-bottle story is told accurately as long as no date is added: the 1921 Swaythling first record was of waxboard tops, not foil (Grokipedia gets this wrong). Fisher and Hinde found the habit began with a few birds and spread by learning, but it was also re-invented in many places, and how it spread (imitation or finding opened bottles) is still debated, so do not write 'copied' or 'imitated' into a context. Eye colour is polygenic but about 98% heritable, so the adopted-child item is fair.
